> This appendix generates the pre-registration of `fba-allergy-online-02`, the
large-scale online replication of @beesley2011, in the Psychological Research
Preregistration-Quantitative (PRP-QUANT) Template, version 4 [@prpquant2026],
with the `{preregr}` package.

The form is structured according to the PreReg web form of the template
(<https://apps.leibniz-psychology.org/prp-quant/>) and rebuilt for `{preregr}`.
This notebook exports its result to the `outputs/` folder: once as a PDF and
once as a state file of the web form (`A1-replication-prereg-zpid.rds`), which
the web form can load via its *Import previous state* functionality, to be
checked there and submitted to PreReg, which is the registry of the Leibniz
Institute for Psychology (ZPID).

::: {.callout-tip title="None of the numbers is typed in by hand"}
Sample sizes, significance thresholds and the decision tree are read from the
design that was exported by the power analysis notebook
(`03-replication-power.qmd`) and the exclusion rules come from the provenance
record of the pilot's `{catlasr}` data bundle, as exported by the feasibility
notebook (`02-feasibility-study.qmd`), apart from the two rules that
`fba-allergy-online-02` rewords. The registration thus cannot drift from the
analyses that justify its contents.
:::

# Specification

Here, I fill the pre-registration form section by section in the collapsed
chunks of R code below. Each item's text is written with `prereg_text()`
function, which fills in the values of the design and joins the lines of every
paragraph. Items marked as not applicable hold the form's not-applicable text,
which the export turns into a ticked *NA* checkbox.

### Introduction (I)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code .hidden}
#| label: replication-prereg-section-i
fba_allergy_online_02 <- preregr::prereg_specify(
  fba_allergy_online_02,

  # Theoretical background
  I1 = prereg_text("
    Forward blocking refers to the attenuation of learning about a cue-outcome
    relationship when the cue is accompanied by another cue that has already
    been established to predict the same outcome [@kamin1969; @dickinson1984;
    @shanks1985]. Although under certain experimental conditions, blocking
    follows from error-driven learning alone [@rescorla1972], eye-tracking and
    behavioural studies suggest that it is often accompanied by learned
    inattention to the blocked cue [@kruschke2005; @lepelley2007; @beesley2011].
    
    Learned-attention models explain it either by rapid attentional shifts or by
    attentional competition [@kruschke2001]. @paskewitz2020 proposed a design
    that could adjudicate between these two explanations, which is yet to be
    experimentally tested. Whereas in the canonical two-stage design, blocking
    can be explained without any attentional mechanism [@sewell2012], in the
    three-stage design of @lepelley2007 and @beesley2011, blocked and control
    cues are paired with new outcomes in a third stage, in the absence of their
    former competitors, so that a deficit in learning about the blocked cue must
    generalise beyond its original association. This design thus requires an
    attentional mechanism [@paskewitz2020] and forms the basis of the planned
    extension study.

    However, blocking may not as reliable as its standing in the literature
    suggests. @maes2016 failed to detect it in fifteen replications of published
    rodent paradigms. The extension of the three-stage design aim at in this
    study is therefore preceded by a replication of its behavioural result in
    the setting in which the extension will run, i.e., an online experiment. A
    pilot study of the present procedure (`fba-allergy-online-01`, see M2) found
    effects in the predicted direction, but was too imprecise to decide about
    its reliability.
  "),

  # Objectives and research questions
  I2 = prereg_text("
    The study has two objectives:

    1. To replicate the blocking effect of @beesley2011, measured by their
    confidence-weighted index on the first test block, in a large online
    sample of participants without prior knowledge of the paradigm.

    2. To select the blocking index for the extension study
    (`fba-allergy-online-03`), with options being the original
    confidence-weighted index or an alternative choice-based index used by the
    simulations of @paskewitz2020.

    The study also provides effect size estimates for the power analysis of the
    extension study.
  "),

  # Hypotheses
  I3 = prereg_text("
    Both hypotheses are tested in the Naive set (i.e., participants showing
    sufficient learning who are unfamiliar with the study design, see AP1),
    one-sided, in the direction of blocking.

    - **H1** (decides the replication). The mean of BI~2~, the
      confidence-weighted blocking index of @beesley2011 on the first test
      block, is greater than zero.

    - **H2** (decides the index of `fba-allergy-online-03`; has no bearing on
      the replication). The mean of BI~3~, the choice-based blocking index of
      @paskewitz2020 over all six test blocks, is greater than zero.

    Both indices are defined in M12. Positive values of either index indicate
    blocking, i.e., test choices of the outcome paired in Stage 3 with the
    control rather than with the blocked cue.
  "),

  # Purely exploratory study
  I3_1 = "No",

  # Exploratory questions
  I4 = prereg_text("
    The test stage is repeated six times, compared to a single block in
    @beesley2011, which allows asking how stable blocking is across the test
    stage (E4) and how reliably the indices measure it (E2 and E3). Indices that
    are robust at the group level may still rank participants unreliably [the
    reliability paradox, @hedge2018], which lowers precision of any later
    correlation estimates of blocking as a trait with other trait-like variables
    (e.g., correlating a behavioural with eye-tracking blocking index by
    @beesley2011).

    - **E1.** Given the sample reached, what are the probabilities of a sign
      error and the expected exaggeration of a significant estimate
      [@gelman2014] under each effect size scenario of M3.2?

    - **E2.** How strongly are BI~2~ and BI~3~ correlated across participants?

    - **E3a.** How strongly are per-block indices correlated between test
      blocks and does the learning check raise these correlations?

    - **E3b.** What is the test-retest reliability (ICC) of the per-block
      indices?

    - **E4a.** Does blocking change across the six test blocks, on average and
      by participant (frequentist mixed models)?

    - **E4b.** If blocking drifts, does it drift towards zero fast enough to
      matter in practice (Bayesian mixed models)?
  ")
)
```

    {{print_power(bi3_look1[['full']])}} if its true effect equals the pilot's

  # Stopping rule

    participants have started the experiment ({{n1_planned}} /

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

**A1 Project description ★**

**Background.** In forward blocking, a cue is learned about less when presented with another cue that already predicts the outcome. In the three-stage design of @beesley2011, blocked cues are also learned about less when paired with new outcomes, indicating selective inattention to the blocked cues.

**Objectives.** To replicate the three-stage blocking effect in a large online sample and to select the blocking index for the extension study to follow.

**Participants.** Students of the LABELS participant pool of Charles University, tested online. Recruitment of 180 participants at look 1, aiming at 90 (at least 72) in the primary analysis set, with a pre-registered top-up at look 2 (see M3).

**Method.** A within-participant three-stage modified allergist task. Blocking is tested by one-sided one-sample *t*-tests of the original index of @beesley2011 and of an alternative choice-based index, in a two-look group-sequential design.

**A2 Keywords ★**

associative learning, cue competition, learned attention, contingency learning, forward blocking, allergist task

**A3 Research area**

Cognitive psychology

## Introduction {.unnumbered}

**I1 Theoretical background**

Forward blocking refers to the attenuation of learning about a cue-outcome relationship when the cue is accompanied by another cue that has already been established to predict the same outcome [@kamin1969; @dickinson1984; @shanks1985]. Although under certain experimental conditions, blocking follows from error-driven learning alone [@rescorla1972], eye-tracking and behavioural studies suggest that it is often accompanied by learned inattention to the blocked cue [@kruschke2005; @lepelley2007; @beesley2011].

Learned-attention models explain it either by rapid attentional shifts or by attentional competition [@kruschke2001]. @paskewitz2020 proposed a design that could adjudicate between these two explanations, which is yet to be experimentally tested. Whereas in the canonical two-stage design, blocking can be explained without any attentional mechanism [@sewell2012], in the three-stage design of @lepelley2007 and @beesley2011, blocked and control cues are paired with new outcomes in a third stage, in the absence of their former competitors, so that a deficit in learning about the blocked cue must generalise beyond its original association. This design thus requires an attentional mechanism [@paskewitz2020] and forms the basis of the planned extension study.

However, blocking may not as reliable as its standing in the literature suggests. @maes2016 failed to detect it in fifteen replications of published rodent paradigms. The extension of the three-stage design aim at in this study is therefore preceded by a replication of its behavioural result in the setting in which the extension will run, i.e., an online experiment. A pilot study of the present procedure (`fba-allergy-online-01`, see M2) found effects in the predicted direction, but was too imprecise to decide about its reliability.

**I2 Objectives and research question(s)**

The study has two objectives:

1. To replicate the blocking effect of @beesley2011, measured by their confidence-weighted index on the first test block, in a large online sample of participants without prior knowledge of the paradigm.

2. To select the blocking index for the extension study (`fba-allergy-online-03`), with options being the original confidence-weighted index or an alternative choice-based index used by the simulations of @paskewitz2020.

The study also provides effect size estimates for the power analysis of the extension study.

**I3 Hypotheses (H1, H2, …) ★**

Both hypotheses are tested in the Naive set (i.e., participants showing sufficient learning who are unfamiliar with the study design, see AP1), one-sided, in the direction of blocking.

- **H1** (decides the replication). The mean of BI~2~, the confidence-weighted blocking index of @beesley2011 on the first test block, is greater than zero.

- **H2** (decides the index of `fba-allergy-online-03`; has no bearing on the replication). The mean of BI~3~, the choice-based blocking index of @paskewitz2020 over all six test blocks, is greater than zero.

Both indices are defined in M12. Positive values of either index indicate blocking, i.e., test choices of the outcome paired in Stage 3 with the control rather than with the blocked cue.

**I3.1 Purely exploratory study**

No

**I4 Exploratory research questions (E1, E2, … - optional)**

The test stage is repeated six times, compared to a single block in @beesley2011, which allows asking how stable blocking is across the test stage (E4) and how reliably the indices measure it (E2 and E3). Indices that are robust at the group level may still rank participants unreliably [the reliability paradox, @hedge2018], which lowers precision of any later correlation estimates of blocking as a trait with other trait-like variables (e.g., correlating a behavioural with eye-tracking blocking index by @beesley2011).

- **E1.** Given the sample reached, what are the probabilities of a sign error and the expected exaggeration of a significant estimate [@gelman2014] under each effect size scenario of M3.2?

- **E2.** How strongly are BI~2~ and BI~3~ correlated across participants?

- **E3a.** How strongly are per-block indices correlated between test blocks and does the learning check raise these correlations?

- **E3b.** What is the test-retest reliability (ICC) of the per-block indices?

- **E4a.** Does blocking change across the six test blocks, on average and by participant (frequentist mixed models)?

- **E4b.** If blocking drifts, does it drift towards zero fast enough to matter in practice (Bayesian mixed models)?

Sample sizes refer to the Naive set (see AP1), unless stated otherwise.

**Look 1.** 180 participants are recruited, aiming at 90 in the Naive set at the assumed retention of 50%, and analysed provided at least 72 reach the set given exclusion criteria (see M3.3).

**Look 2** (only if neither index detects blocking at look 1, see M3.3 and AP10). The Naive set is brought to the sample *n*~2~ set by the rule of M3.3: 441 participants at the assumed 50% retention, about 882 recruited in total. The rule at the four retention rates illustrated in the power analysis:

- 40% retention: 72 at look 1, 452 at look 2 (1130 recruited in total), nominal one-sided *p* < .0068
- 50% retention: 90 at look 1, 441 at look 2 (882 recruited in total), nominal one-sided *p* < .0073
- 60% retention: 108 at look 1, 429 at look 2 (715 recruited in total), nominal one-sided *p* < .0078
- 75% retention: 135 at look 1, 410 at look 2 (547 recruited in total), nominal one-sided *p* < .0088

**M3.2 Sample size justification ★**

**Effect size scenarios.** Sample sizes are planned for BI~2~ (H1) in the Naive set, for a one-sided one-sample *t*-test at α = .05, under three scenarios of the true standardised mean *d*~z~: *Best* [0.54, @beesley2011], *Realistic* (0.35, the pilot's Full sample) and *Worst* (0.15, the pilot's Naive set). A single test needs 72 participants for 90% power under the *Realistic* scenario and 90 for 95%.

**Retention.** The retention, i.e., the share of recruited participants who reach the final Naive set, is assumed to be 50%. In the pilot study, it was 8 of 20 (40%) overall and 5 of 10 (50%) among participants of the LABELS pool.

**Design.** The study is a two-look group-sequential design [@wassmer2025], planned according to design calculations using the `rpact` R package [@wassmer2026] with *t*-based power (see M3.3 for the looks specification). With 90 participants, look 1 has 95% power under the *Realistic* and 39% under the *Worst* scenario. Look 2 is sized for 80% overall power across both looks under the *Worst* scenario.

**BI~3~** (H2) is tested at the same looks against the same boundaries. With 90 participants at look 1, its power is 94% if its true effect equals the pilot's Full sample estimate (*d*~z~ = 0.34) and 83% if it equals the Learned set estimate (*d*~z~ = 0.28).

**Precision.** If the true effect equals the *Realistic* scenario, the 90% confidence interval of *d*~z~ at 90 participants is expected to be [0.17, 0.53].

The power analysis is documented in the notebook *3 · Experiment 1: Power Analysis* (`03-replication-power.qmd`) of the `CATLAS` repository.

**M3.3 Stopping rule ★**

**Look 1** is the replication proper. Recruitment closes once 180 participants have started the experiment (90 / 0.5), and the data are analysed once recruitment has closed, provided at least 72 of them reach the final Naive set. If fewer participants do, recruitment continues in batches sized to reach 90 at the retention observed so far, until at least 72 reach the Naive set. Look 1 spends a fixed one-sided α~1~ = .045.

**Look 2** takes place if and only if neither BI~2~ nor BI~3~ detects blocking at look 1 (see AP10). It brings the Naive set to the smallest sample *n*~2~ that gives the design 80% overall power across both looks under the *Worst* scenario, given the look-1 sample *n*~1~ actually reached. The number of participants recruited for look 2 assumes the retention observed at look 1. If fewer than *n*~2~ then reach the Naive set, recruitment continues in batches, as at look 1. Only these outcome-blind quantities, i.e., the sample reached and the retention, enter the sampling rule; the look-1 blocking estimates never do. At the assumed retention, look 2 rejects the null hypothesis at a nominal one-sided *p* < .0073 (see M3.1 for other retention rates).

**Cap on look 2.** If the rule specified above asks for more participants than the LABELS pool can supply in one semester, look 2 stops at the largest available sample size, and the power it achieves is reported.

**Critical values** are recomputed for the samples actually reached at each look, keeping α~1~ = .045 and the overall α = .05.

**No other look** at either blocking index is planned. Attrition, completion time and the yield of the learning check are monitored during data collection (see M7).

## Method - Conditions and design {.unnumbered}

**M9 Research method ★**

Experiment

**M9.1 Experimental design**

Design with repeated measures (only "within-subject" variables)

**M9.1.1 Conditions and their implementation**

An experimental, cross-sectional study with a single group and a within-participant three-stage forward blocking design [@lepelley2007; @beesley2011], specified as the `three-stage-replication` design of `catlasr` and illustrated in Table 1 of the manuscript. Each stage consists of blocks of eight trial types.

- **Stage 1** (elemental training): four blocking cues and four filler cues, each paired with one of two outcomes (o1, o2).

- **Stage 2** (compound training): each blocking cue in compound with a new cue (the blocked cues), and four compounds of two new cues (one of them a control cue), paired with o1 or o2.

- **Stage 3** (novel learning): four compounds of one blocked and one control cue, paired with two new outcomes (o3, o4), and four filler compounds of new cues.

- **Test**: eight pairs of one blocked and one control cue that were paired with different outcomes in Stage 3. Blocking predicts preference for the choice of the control cue's outcome.

The factor of interest, cue status (blocked or control), is thus manipulated within participants and test pairs.

**M10 Multilevel structure**

Trial-level responses are nested within crossed by-participant and by-test-pair clusters. The confirmatory tests (AP8) use one value of each index per participant; the exploratory mixed models (E4a, E4b) model the trial level.

**M11 Randomization of participants and/or experimental materials**

Independently for each participant, the 28 cue roles are randomly assigned the names of 28 fictitious chemicals, and the four outcomes are randomly assigned the four side effects (dizziness, itchiness, headache, nausea). Within every block, the order of the eight trial types is randomised, with the constraint that no trial type repeats across a block boundary. The left-right order of the two cues of a compound is counterbalanced across the blocks of Stages 2 and 3 and of the test stage. The screen position of the outcomes is fixed (o1 and o3 left, o2 and o4 right).

**M12 Variables used in the confirmatory analyses ★**

**Dependent variables.** On every test trial, the outcome chosen (one of the two Stage 3 outcomes) and the confidence in the choice (1, *Not confident at all*, to 10, *Very confident*). From these, the signed confidence of a trial is the confidence if the participant chose the outcome paired in Stage 3 with the control cue of the pair, and minus the confidence otherwise.

- **BI~2~** [@beesley2011]: the mean signed confidence over the answered trials of the first test block, i.e., of 8 trials (from −10 to 10; `catlasr::index_blocking(blocks = 1)`, column `bi_confidence`). It is the index of H1.

- **BI~3~** [@paskewitz2020]: over the answered trials of all six test blocks, i.e., of up to 48 trials, the sum across the eight test pairs of the proportion of choices of the control cue's outcome, minus one half per pair (from −4 to 4; `catlasr::index_blocking(blocks = NULL)`, column `bi_choice`). It is the index of H2.

**Independent variable.** Cue status (blocked or control), manipulated within participants (M9.1.1); the indices contrast the two.

**M13 Other variables ★**

Accuracy and response times of the learning trials (the learning check of AP1), response times of the test trials, the two debriefing answers and whether the debriefing timed out (AP1, rule 5), age and sex (sample description only), and the duration of the run. An optional free-text comment at the end of the debriefing is neither imported nor analysed. No covariates enter the confirmatory analyses.

**M17 Study procedures**

The procedure follows @beesley2011, a variant of the allergist task [@dickinson1996; @lochmann2003]. A browser check first turns away devices whose browser reports itself as mobile (mostly phones). A welcome screen, which asks participants to reserve about 25 to 30 minutes, a stable internet connection and a quiet environment, and four screens of study information precede the informed consent. Declining consent ends the experiment and deletes the data recorded so far. Participants may then enter an e-mail address for the course credit (M4.5), state their sex and age (both required, with no answer preselected), and read the instructions, which include animated tutorials and requests not to take notes and to focus on correct rather than fast responses. Stage 1 has 10 blocks (80 trials), Stage 2 has 8 blocks (64 trials), Stage 3 has 6 blocks (48 trials) and the test stage has 6 blocks (48 trials). On every trial, participants click the image of the side effect they predict and confirm with an OK button. In Stages 1–3, the words *Correct* (green) or *Wrong* (red) and a frame around the correct image follow every response for 1.5 seconds. In the test stage, there is no feedback and every choice is followed by the confidence rating. Stage 3 introduces a new patient, with a new instruction text. A learning trial without a response ends after 60 seconds. A test trial ends as unanswered after 60 seconds unless both the choice and the confidence rating are given. Instruction screens end after 180 seconds and the consent screen has no time limit. The experiment ends with the debriefing questions of AP1 (rule 5), whose screen also ends after 180 seconds, an optional comment, and a farewell screen that serves as the confirmation of participation (M4.5).

## Analysis plan {.unnumbered}

**AP1 Criteria for exclusion of participants & outlier treatment ★**

**Inclusion criteria for data collection.** Students of the LABELS pool (M4.2) who are at least 18 years old, did not take part in the pilot `fba-allergy-online-01`, and run the experiment on a laptop or desktop computer.

**Exclusion criteria.** Participants are excluded by the following rules, applied in the order listed. An excluded participant is counted under the first rule that removes them. Rules 2–4 are worded verbatim as in the provenance record of the pilot's data. Rule 1 is reworded because declining consent now deletes the data recorded until that point and it is applied first so that a declined run is not counted under rule 2. Rule 5 is reworded for the new debriefing question.

1. **Declined consent.** The participant declined on the informed-consent screen. Declining ends the experiment and deletes the data recorded so far, so that JATOS keeps only the study result, in the state ABORTED.
2. **No jsPsych data.** The JATOS study result holds no jsPsych data that can be parsed, for instance because the study link was opened but no trial record reached the server.
3. **Incomplete run.** The run does not contain at least one complete test block of 8 trials.
4. **Insufficient learning.** The participant did not score significantly above chance in at least one of the three learning stages, as decided by a one-sided exact binomial test of the number of correct responses against 0.5 at alpha = 0.10 over all answered trials of the stage (timed-out trials excluded). On complete data, fewer than 47 of 80 correct in Stage 1, 38 of 64 in Stage 2, or 29 of 48 in Stage 3. A stage without any answered trial counts as failed.
5. **Prior knowledge.** The participant answered yes to the debriefing question "Before today, have you taken part in an experiment in which you predicted reactions from foods or medicines?", their answer to the debriefing question "Did you know or guess what this study tested? If so, describe it." was coded as describing blocking, or the debriefing screen timed out or was not reached. An answer describes blocking if it states that learning about a cue is reduced when the cue is presented together with a cue that already predicts the outcome, or if it names blocking, cue competition or learned (in)attention. Answers that describe only the surface of the task (predicting side effects, memory, attention or learning in general) do not. The answers are coded before any blocking index is computed.

The debriefing questions of rule 5 are shown in Czech: "Účastnil/a jste se již před dneškem experimentu, ve kterém jste předpovídal/a reakce na potraviny nebo léky?" (*Ano* / *Ne*) and "Věděl/a jste nebo tušil/a, co tato studie zkoumala? Pokud ano, popište to." Both are compulsory: the screen cannot be left before the first is answered and the second holds text.

The rules define three nested analysis sets: the **Full sample** (after rules 1–3), the **Learned set** (after rules 1–4) and the **Naive set** (after rules 1–5). The Naive set is the primary analysis set and alone tests H1 and H2. The other two serve the sensitivity analyses of AP8. Rules 4 and 5 are blind to the test data (see M6).

**Outliers.** No participant is excluded as an outlier on any variable. An excluded participant is excluded from all analyses of the sets that the rule removes them from.

**AP2 Criteria for post-data collection exclusions on trial or item level ★**

Only timed-out trials, i.e., trials without a response within 60 seconds, are excluded (see AP5). No trials are excluded for their response times.

**AP3 Exhaustiveness of exclusion criteria ★**

All exclusion criteria (on the participant and trial/item level) that are currently planned are listed above.

**AP4 Data preprocessing**

The JATOS study results are imported, validated and anonymised with the `catlasr` R package (PD8), and downloaded with `pull_jatos_batches()`. During the experiment, every trial is streamed to JATOS upon its end and, at the end of a run, the complete jsPsych data are also uploaded as the result file `jspsych-data.json` (`result_file = "jspsych-data.json"`). For every study result (i.e., run), the result file is read where it exists and the streamed data only where it does not (unfinished runs, failed uploads) or cannot be parsed. The two are never combined and the source of every study result is recorded (as `data_source`) and reported. Before any exclusion, the JATOS identifiers are replaced by random six-digit participant IDs (via `update_id_key()`), whose key is kept in a private folder. The e-mail addresses are kept apart from the responses (M4.5).

Data bundle validation (via `validate_fba_rawdata()`) must pass before any analysis. The exclusion rules of AP1 are recorded in the provenance record of the data set with the `record_exclusion()` function, in the order they are applied. The learning check of rule 4 is computed with `test_learning(alpha = 0.10)` and `screen_learning(rule = "any")`. For rule 5, `write_debrief_coding()` writes a coding file that contains only the participant IDs and the debriefing answers, and `read_debrief_coding()` reads the codes back; the data import does not proceed until every answer is coded. Test trials are scored with `score_blocking()`, which signs every answered trial by whether its choice is consistent with blocking, and the indices of M12 are computed per participant with `index_blocking()`: BI~2~ on the first test block, BI~3~ over all test blocks, and both per test block (`by_block = TRUE`) for the exploratory analyses. The indices are not screened for outliers, transformed or winsorised.

**AP5 How will missing data be handled?**

**Definition.** A learning trial without a response ends after 60 seconds, and so does a test trial in which the choice and the confidence rating are not both given. Timed-out trials have no response and enter neither the learning check (rule 4 of AP1) nor the calculation of the blocking indices, which average over answered trials only. A participant's BI~2~ is missing if every trial of the first test block timed out and their BI~3~ if a given test pair has no answered trial. Both debriefing questions, upon which prior knowledge of the design is established, are compulsory, but the debriefing screen ends after 180 seconds. A participant whose debriefing timed out or was not reached is excluded from the Naive set by rule 5 of AP1.

**Handling.** A participant whose BI~2~ is missing is left out of the test of H1, and a participant whose BI~3~ is missing is left out of the test of H2 (case-wise deletion per analysis). Missing data are not imputed.

**Missingness mechanism.** Whether trials are missing at random is not tested. The number of timed-out trials and of participants left out is reported.

**AP6 Reliability analysis (if applicable)**

The reliability of the indices across the six test blocks is estimated in the exploratory analyses E3a and E3b (AP11). It does not enter the confirmatory analyses.

**AP7 Descriptive statistics**

For the recruited sample: the number of participants removed by each exclusion rule; the age and sex of every analysis set, in aggregate only; the duration of the run. For the learning stages: the accuracy per stage and block, by cue type (learning curves). For each index and analysis set: the mean and standard deviation (`aggregate_blocking()`), the 90% confidence interval of the mean, and *d*~z~ (mean divided by standard deviation) with its exact 90% confidence interval, obtained by inverting the noncentral *t* distribution. 90% CIs are selected instead of their more typical 95% counterparts because the former align better with the one-sided test applied to the data. Finally, per-block means of both indices are plotted across the six test blocks.

**AP8 Statistical models (for each hypothesis if varies) ★**

**H1.** One-sided one-sample *t*-test of the per-participant BI~2~ (`index_blocking()`, AP4) against zero (alternative: mean greater than zero), in the Naive set, at each look of M3.3. At look 2, the test uses all participants of the Naive set (looks 1 and 2 together) and the critical value of the two-look design, computed with `rpact::getAnalysisResults()` from the stage-wise sample sizes, means and standard deviations (*t*-based, version 4.4.0 at registration).

**H2.** The same test of the per-participant BI~3~, at the same looks and boundaries.

**Correction for multiple testing.** BI~2~ and BI~3~ are not corrected for each other, because they decide different questions: only BI~2~ decides the replication, only BI~3~'s result decides which index the extension study uses (AP10). The two looks are corrected by the α spending of M3.3.

**Sensitivity analyses.** *d*~z~ with its 90% confidence interval for both indices in the Full sample and in the Learned set. These estimates are reported, but do not decide anything.

**Estimates after look 2.** If the study stops at look 2, the effect is reported as the median-unbiased estimate with its confidence interval under the stage-wise ordering, which correct the bias of the naive estimate after a sequential design, alongside the naive estimate.

**AP9 Assumption tests**

**One-sample *t*-tests (H1, H2).** Normality of the per-participant indices is not tested; the one-sample *t*-test is applied regardless on the basis of the central limit theorem, following established practice of previous forward blocking experimental studies. Independence of participants holds by design. No transformations or non-parametric alternatives are planned.

**Mixed models (E4a).** Singular fits are refitted without the correlation of the random effects and, if still singular, left out (see AP11).

**AP10 Inference criteria**

An index **passes** at a look if its one-sided test rejects the null hypothesis of no blocking at the threshold of that look: one-sided *p* < .045 at look 1, and below the nominal threshold of the recomputed look-2 critical value at look 2 (about .007 at the 50% assumed retention, see M3.3). H1 and H2 are separate hypotheses without sub-hypotheses. The result of BI~2~ alone decides whether the replication succeeds (H1); the result of BI~3~ alone decides which index carries on to `fba-allergy-online-03`. The decision tree:

- **Look 1** (one-sided *p* < .045): BI~2~ passes, BI~3~ passes. Replication: **SUCCESS**. Next step: `fba-allergy-online-03` with BI~3~ (no top-up).
- **Look 1** (one-sided *p* < .045): BI~2~ passes, BI~3~ fails. Replication: **SUCCESS**. Next step: `fba-allergy-online-03` with BI~2~ (no top-up).
- **Look 1** (one-sided *p* < .045): BI~2~ fails, BI~3~ passes. Replication: **FAILURE**. Next step: `fba-allergy-online-03` with BI~3~ (no top-up).
- **Look 1** (one-sided *p* < .045): BI~2~ fails, BI~3~ fails. Replication: **Undecided**. Next step: Look 2 (top-up of the sample).
- **Look 2** (one-sided *p* < .007): BI~2~ passes, BI~3~ passes. Replication: **SUCCESS**. Next step: `fba-allergy-online-03` with BI~3~.
- **Look 2** (one-sided *p* < .007): BI~2~ passes, BI~3~ fails. Replication: **SUCCESS**. Next step: `fba-allergy-online-03` with BI~2~ (theorise why BI~2~ was the more sensitive index).
- **Look 2** (one-sided *p* < .007): BI~2~ fails, BI~3~ passes. Replication: **FAILURE**. Next step: `fba-allergy-online-03` with BI~3~.
- **Look 2** (one-sided *p* < .007): BI~2~ fails, BI~3~ fails. Replication: **FAILURE**. Next step: Change course (no `fba-allergy-online-03` extension).

A failure at look 2 of both indices ends the online line of studies: the next step is a laboratory replication with eye tracking. No smallest effect size of interest is defined. The design is planned for 80% overall power at *d*~z~ = 0.15, the smallest of the scenarios. For the extension study, *d*~z~ of the selected index is reported with its 95% confidence interval, because the extension study tests a two-sided hypothesis adjudicating between two competing theories.

**AP11 Exploratory analyses (optional)**

The following analyses are exploratory and are reported as such, in every analysis set.

- **E1.** A design analysis [@gelman2014] of each index at the sample reached, giving the probability of a sign error (Type S) and the expected exaggeration ratio (Type M) of a significant estimate under each of the three scenarios of M3.2.

- **E2.** Pearson's correlation of the per-participant BI~2~ and BI~3~, with its 95% confidence interval.

- **E3a.** The 6 × 6 matrices of Pearson's correlations of the per-block indices between test blocks, for each index. Higher correlations in the Learned and Naive sets than in the Full sample would suggest that the learning check raises between-block reliability.

- **E3b.** Intraclass correlations of the per-block indices across the six test blocks, for each index: two-way, consistency, single block (ICC(3,1)) and mean of six blocks (ICC(3,6)), with 95% confidence intervals.

- **E4a.** Three nested mixed models of the trial-level data of each index, fitted with `{lme4}`: signed confidence (BI~2~) as Gaussian and the blocking-consistent choice (BI~3~) as binomial with a logit link, with crossed by-participant and by-test-pair random intercepts, and (1) no change across test blocks, (2) a common linear drift (test block coded 0–5), (3) an additional by-participant drift. Singular fits are refitted without the correlation of the random effects and, if still singular, left out. The models are compared by likelihood-ratio tests and AIC.

- **E4b.** Bayesian versions of the three models, fitted in Stan with weakly informative default priors as in `{rstanarm}`, for the choice (binomial, logit link) and for the unsigned confidence (ordinal, cumulative logit), with linear drift only. If blocking drifts towards zero, the extrapolated test block at which the drift line of the choice model crosses zero is evaluated by the posterior probability that the slope is greater than minus the intercept divided by 9, i.e., that the line crosses zero after the 10th test block (and, likewise, after the 6th block, dividing by 5). A crossing after the 10th block is taken as practically insignificant drift. The slopes of the choice and confidence models are compared.

**AP12 Other information**

Deviations from this registration are reported and justified in the manuscript.

## Other information {.unnumbered}

**O1 Other information**

**Deviations from the pilot `fba-allergy-online-01`.**

- Data are uploaded in full at the end of the experiment, in addition to trial by trial, so that a lost connection no longer loses data.

- Test trials end after 60 seconds unless both the choice and the confidence rating are given; in the pilot, they had no time limit, yet none of its test trials took that long.

- Declining consent aborts the JATOS run, which deletes the data recorded so far, and the consent screen has no time limit. In the pilot, a declined run kept its data, and the consent screen ended after 120 seconds, after which the experiment continued. The consent rule of AP1 is reworded and applied first accordingly.

- The single debriefing question about taking part in a similar experiment is replaced by the two compulsory questions of rule 5 of AP1, and the exclusion rule is reworded accordingly, with a coding rule for the free text. The debriefing screen ends after 180 seconds, and a timed-out debriefing excludes the participant from the Naive set.

- The Naive set is the primary analysis set; in the pilot, it was the Learned set. The prior-knowledge exclusion removes participants who may answer from what they expect the study to show, which the pilot could not afford with its small sample.

- Participants are recruited from the LABELS pool only (the pilot also recruited personal contacts), among students who did not take part in the pilot.

**Deviations from @beesley2011.** The study runs online rather than in the laboratory and without eye tracking, in Czech. The test stage is repeated six times instead of once. The original index (BI~2~) uses the first test block only, so that it remains comparable. Participants who do not learn reliably above chance or report prior knowledge are excluded, which @beesley2011 did not do.

#' @param .envir Environment in which the expressions are evaluated.
#'
#' @returns Character(1).
prereg_text <- function(..., .envir = parent.frame()) {
  x <- glue::glue(..., .envir = .envir, .open = "{{", .close = "}}")
  x <- gsub("(?m)^[ \\t]+|[ \\t]+$", "", x, perl = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("(?<=\\S)\\n(?!\\n|- |[0-9]+\\. )", " ", x, perl = TRUE)
  trimws(as.character(x))
}


#' Exclusion rules of the registered study
#'
#' Lists the exclusion rules in the order they are applied, with their wording
#' taken verbatim from a provenance record, except for the rules whose wording
#' the registered study revises.
#'
#' @param exclusions The `exclusions` element of a `{catlasr}` provenance
#'   record, i.e., a list with one element per rule, each with `rule` and
#'   `description`.
#' @param rule_labels Named character. The label of every rule, named by rule
#'   and in the order of `exclusions`.
#' @param revised Named character. The new wording of the revised rules, named
#'   by rule.
#'
#' @returns Character, one Markdown list item per rule.
write_prereg_rules <- function(
    exclusions,
    rule_labels,
    revised = character()
) {
  rules <- purrr::map_chr(exclusions, "rule")
  stopifnot(
    identical(unname(rules), names(rule_labels)),
    all(names(revised) %in% rules)
  )
  
  descriptions <- rlang::set_names(purrr::map_chr(exclusions, "description"), rules)
  descriptions[names(revised)] <- revised
  
  sprintf(
    "%d. **%s.** %s",
    seq_along(rules),
    rule_labels[rules],
    descriptions
  )
}


#' Decision tree of the registered study as a list
#'
#' @param decisions A tibble with one row per look and combination of test
#'   results: `look`, `bi2` and `bi3` (`"pass"` or `"fail"`), `replication`,
#'   `next_step` and `note`, as exported by the power analysis notebook.
#' @param thresholds Character(2). The one-sided significance thresholds of
#'   looks 1 and 2 as printed, e.g. `c("< .045", "< .007")`.
#'
#' @returns Character, one Markdown list item per row of `decisions`.
write_prereg_decisions <- function(decisions, thresholds) {
  outcome <- function(x) dplyr::if_else(x == "pass", "passes", "fails")
  
  study_names <- function(x) {
    x |>
      stringr::str_replace_all("(?<![\\w-])-03\\b", "`fba-allergy-online-03`") |>
      stringr::str_replace_all("BI([23])", "BI~\\1~")
  }
  
  note <- dplyr::if_else(
    is.na(decisions$note),
    "",
    paste0(" (", study_names(decisions$note), ")")
  )
  
  sprintf(
    "- **Look %d** (one-sided *p* %s): BI~2~ %s, BI~3~ %s. Replication: **%s**. Next step: %s%s.",
    decisions$look,
    thresholds[decisions$look],
    outcome(decisions$bi2),
    outcome(decisions$bi3),
    decisions$replication,
    study_names(decisions$next_step),
    note
  )
}

#' Items of a pre-registration with their answers
#'
#' @param x A `{preregr}` (pre)registration object, as returned by
#'   [preregr::prereg_initialize()] and filled by [preregr::prereg_specify()].
#'
#' @returns A tibble with one row per item: the item columns of the form
#'   (without the `item_` prefix), `text` (`NA` when unspecified), and `shown`,
#'   whether the web form shows the item given the answers.
prereg_items <- function(x) {
  items <- tibble::as_tibble(x$form$items)
  names(items) <- sub("^item_", "", names(items))

  text <- purrr::map_chr(items$id, \(id) x$specs[[id]]$text)
  text[text == x$config$initialText] <- NA_character_
  items$text <- text

  if (!"shown_if_id" %in% names(items)) {
    items$shown <- TRUE
    return(items)
  }

  # An item is shown if it has no condition, or if the item it depends on is
  # shown and holds (or, with several options, includes) the value
  holds <- function(id, value) {
    answer <- items$text[match(id, items$id)]
    if (is.na(answer)) return(FALSE)
    value %in% trimws(strsplit(answer, ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1L]])
  }
  shown <- is.na(items$shown_if_id)
  repeat {
    previous <- shown
    shown <- is.na(items$shown_if_id) | purrr::map2_lgl(
      items$shown_if_id, items$shown_if_value,
      \(id, value) !is.na(id) && shown[match(id, items$id)] && holds(id, value)
    )
    if (identical(shown, previous)) break
  }
  items$shown <- shown

  items
}


#' Completion of the pre-registration form
#'
#' @param x A `{preregr}` (pre)registration object.
#' @param flag Character. Markers of content still to be decided or added.
#'
#' @returns A tibble with one row per item that needs attention: `item`,
#'   `label` and `status`, which is one of "Required, unspecified" (a required
#'   item that the web form shows), "Optional, unspecified", "Hidden but
#'   specified" (an item that the web form does not show given the answers, so
#'   its text would be lost), or "To decide" (text holding one of `flag`).
check_prereg <- function(x, flag = c("[To decide", "[To add")) {
  items <- prereg_items(x)
  required <- if ("required" %in% names(items)) items$required else TRUE
  flagged <- purrr::map_lgl(
    items$text,
    \(t) !is.na(t) && any(vapply(flag, \(f) grepl(f, t, fixed = TRUE), logical(1)))
  )

  tibble::tibble(
    item   = items$id,
    label  = items$label,
    status = dplyr::case_when(
      !items$shown & !is.na(items$text) ~ "Hidden but specified",
      !items$shown ~ NA_character_,
      is.na(items$text) & required ~ "Required, unspecified",
      is.na(items$text) ~ "Optional, unspecified",
      flagged ~ "To decide",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(status))
}


#' Path to the Quarto command-line tool
#'
#' Quarto bundles the pandoc and typst binaries that the conversions and the
#' PDF export use.
#'
#' @returns Character(1), the path to the `quarto` executable.
find_quarto <- function() {
  candidates <- c(
    Sys.getenv("QUARTO_PATH"),
    if (requireNamespace("quarto", quietly = TRUE)) {
      tryCatch(quarto::quarto_path(), error = function(e) "")
    },
    Sys.which("quarto"),
    "/Applications/quarto/bin/quarto",
    "/Applications/RStudio.app/Contents/Resources/app/quarto/bin/quarto",
    "/usr/local/bin/quarto",
    "/opt/quarto/bin/quarto"
  )
  candidates <- candidates[nzchar(candidates) & file.exists(candidates)]
  if (length(candidates) == 0L) {
    stop(
      "Quarto was not found. Set the QUARTO_PATH environment variable to the ",
      "path of the quarto executable."
    )
  }
  unname(candidates[[1L]])
}


#' Run a Quarto subcommand
#'
#' @param args Character. The arguments, e.g. `c("pandoc", "in.md", ...)`.
#'
#' @returns Invisibly, the standard output. Stops with the error output if the
#'   command fails.
run_quarto <- function(args) {
  err <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
  out <- suppressWarnings(system2(
    find_quarto(),
    args = shQuote(args),
    stdout = TRUE,
    stderr = err
  ))
  status <- attr(out, "status")
  if (!is.null(status) && status != 0L) {
    stop(
      "Quarto failed (quarto ", paste(args, collapse = " "), "):\n",
      paste(readLines(err, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
    )
  }
  invisible(out)
}


#' Citation keys of a pre-registration
#'
#' @param x A `{preregr}` (pre)registration object.
#' @param bibliography Character(1). Path to the BibTeX file.
#'
#' @returns Character, the keys of the bibliography that the items cite (as
#'   `@key`), in order of first citation.
prereg_cited_keys <- function(x, bibliography) {
  items <- prereg_items(x)
  text <- paste(stats::na.omit(items$text[items$shown]), collapse = "\n")
  cited <- regmatches(
    text,
    gregexpr("(?<![\\w.@])@([A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_:.#$%&+?<>~/-]*[A-Za-z0-9_])", text, perl = TRUE)
  )[[1L]]
  cited <- unique(sub("^@", "", cited))

  bib <- readLines(bibliography, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  keys <- sub("^\\s*@\\w+\\s*\\{\\s*([^,]+),.*$", "\\1", grep("^\\s*@\\w+\\s*\\{", bib, value = TRUE))
  missing <- setdiff(cited, keys)
  if (length(missing) > 0L) {
    warning(
      "Cited but not in the bibliography: ",
      paste0("@", missing, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }
  intersect(cited, keys)
}


#' Convert Markdown texts with pandoc, resolving citations
#'
#' @param texts Named character. The Markdown texts, e.g. item answers.
#' @param bibliography Character(1). Path to the BibTeX file.
#' @param csl Character(1). Path to the citation style.
#' @param to Character(1). The pandoc output format, e.g. `"plain"` or
#'   `"markdown"`.
#'
#' @returns A list: `texts` (named character, the converted texts) and
#'   `references` (character(1), the list of the cited references).
prereg_convert <- function(texts, bibliography, csl, to = "plain") {
  marker <- "PREREGITEMMARKER"
  body <- paste0(
    marker, " ", names(texts), "\n\n", texts,
    collapse = "\n\n"
  )
  # A subscript z has no Unicode character; plain text writes d_z instead of
  # pandoc's d_(z)
  if (to == "plain") {
    body <- gsub("~z~", "_z", body, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  md <- paste0(
    body, "\n\n", marker, " REFLIST\n\n::: {#refs}\n:::\n"
  )

  input <- tempfile(fileext = ".md")
  output <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
  writeLines(md, input, useBytes = TRUE)
  run_quarto(c(
    "pandoc", input,
    "--from", "markdown",
    "--to", to,
    "--citeproc",
    "--bibliography", normalizePath(bibliography),
    "--csl", normalizePath(csl),
    "--wrap", "none",
    "--output", output
  ))

  lines <- readLines(output, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  starts <- grep(paste0("^\\\\?", marker, " "), lines)
  ids <- sub(paste0("^\\\\?", marker, " "), "", lines[starts])
  ids <- gsub("\\\\", "", ids)
  ends <- c(starts[-1L] - 1L, length(lines))
  chunks <- purrr::map2_chr(starts, ends, \(s, e) {
    if (e <= s) return("")
    out <- paste(lines[(s + 1L):e], collapse = "\n")
    # Pandoc's Markdown writer wraps the reference list in fenced divs
    out <- gsub("(?m)^:{3,}.*$", "", out, perl = TRUE)
    trimws(gsub("\n{3,}", "\n\n", out))
  })
  names(chunks) <- ids

  list(
    texts = chunks[setdiff(ids, "REFLIST")],
    references = chunks[["REFLIST"]]
  )
}


#' Reference list of a pre-registration
#'
#' @inheritParams prereg_cited_keys
#' @param csl Character(1). Path to the citation style, e.g. APA.
#'
#' @returns Character(1), the formatted references in Markdown, one paragraph
#'   per reference.
prereg_references <- function(x, bibliography, csl) {
  keys <- prereg_cited_keys(x, bibliography)
  if (length(keys) == 0L) {
    return("")
  }
  cites <- purrr::set_names(paste0("[@", keys, "]"), keys)
  prereg_convert(cites, bibliography, csl, to = "markdown")$references
}


#' A pre-registration as a Markdown document
#'
#' Lists the items the web form shows, by section, with their template number,
#' label and answer. Unspecified items are marked as such; the citations stay
#' as `@key`, to be resolved by whatever renders the document.
#'
#' @param x A `{preregr}` (pre)registration object.
#' @param exclude Character. Items to leave out, e.g. `"R1"` when the renderer
#'   builds the reference list itself.
#' @param heading_level Integer(1). The level of the section headings.
#' @param item_style Character(1). `"heading"` gives every item a heading one
#'   level below its section; `"bold"` a bold label, which keeps the items out
#'   of a table of contents.
#'
#' @returns Character(1).
prereg_to_markdown <- function(
    x,
    exclude = character(),
    heading_level = 1L,
    item_style = c("heading", "bold")
) {
  item_style <- match.arg(item_style)
  items <- prereg_items(x)
  items <- items[items$shown & !items$id %in% exclude, ]
  sections <- x$form$sections
  title <- if ("title" %in% names(items)) items$title else items$label
  number <- if ("number" %in% names(items)) items$number else items$id
  required <- if ("required" %in% names(items)) items$required else FALSE
  h1 <- strrep("#", heading_level)
  h2 <- strrep("#", heading_level + 1L)

  blocks <- purrr::map_chr(seq_len(nrow(items)), function(i) {
    answer <- if (is.na(items$text[i])) "*Unspecified.*" else items$text[i]
    if (identical(items$type[i], "checkboxgroup") && !is.na(items$text[i])) {
      answer <- paste0("- ", trimws(strsplit(answer, ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1L]]), collapse = "\n")
    }
    label <- paste0(
      if (nzchar(number[i])) paste0(number[i], " ") else "",
      title[i],
      if (isTRUE(required[i])) " \u2605" else ""
    )
    if (item_style == "heading") {
      sprintf("%s %s {.unnumbered}\n\n%s", h2, label, answer)
    } else {
      sprintf("**%s**\n\n%s", label, answer)
    }
  })

  section_of <- items$section_id
  out <- character()
  for (s in unique(section_of)) {
    label <- sections$section_label[match(s, sections$section_id)]
    out <- c(out, sprintf("%s %s {.unnumbered}", h1, label), blocks[section_of == s])
  }
  paste(out, collapse = "\n\n")
}


#' Export a pre-registration to PDF
#'
#' Converts the Markdown of [prereg_to_markdown()] with pandoc to typst,
#' resolving the citations and appending the reference list, and compiles it
#' with typst, both as bundled with Quarto.
#'
#' @param x A `{preregr}` (pre)registration object.
#' @param file Character(1). The PDF file to write.
#' @param title,subtitle Character(1). The title and subtitle of the document.
#' @param bibliography Character(1). Path to the BibTeX file.
#' @param csl Character(1). Path to the citation style.
#' @param contributors Optional tibble of contributors, as for
#'   [write_prereg_contributors()], named as authors.
#'
#' @returns Invisibly, `file`.
prereg_to_pdf <- function(
    x,
    file,
    title,
    subtitle = NULL,
    bibliography,
    csl,
    contributors = NULL
) {
  stopifnot(dir.exists(dirname(file)))

  yaml_string <- function(s) paste0("\"", gsub("\"", "\\\\\"", s), "\"")
  header <- c(
    "---",
    paste0("title: ", yaml_string(title)),
    if (!is.null(subtitle)) {
      paste0("subtitle: ", yaml_string(subtitle))
    },
    if (!is.null(contributors)) {
      c("author:", paste0("  - ", yaml_string(contributors$name)))
    },
    paste0(
      "date: ", yaml_string(format(Sys.Date(), "%d %B %Y"))
    ),
    "papersize: a4",
    "---"
    )
  body <- prereg_to_markdown(x, exclude = "R1")
  md <- paste(
    c(header, "", body, "", "# References {.unnumbered}", "", "::: {#refs}", ":::"),
    collapse = "\n"
  )

  dir <- tempfile("prereg-pdf-")
  dir.create(dir)
  input <- file.path(dir, "prereg.md")
  typ <- file.path(dir, "prereg.typ")
  pdf <- file.path(dir, "prereg.pdf")
  writeLines(md, input, useBytes = TRUE)

  run_quarto(c(
    "pandoc", input,
    "--from", "markdown",
    "--to", "typst",
    "--standalone",
    "--citeproc",
    "--bibliography", normalizePath(bibliography),
    "--csl", normalizePath(csl),
    "--output", typ
  ))
  run_quarto(c("typst", "compile", typ, pdf))

  file.copy(pdf, file, overwrite = TRUE)
  invisible(file)
}


#' Export a pre-registration as a state file of the PreReg web form
#'
#' Writes the `.rds` file that the PreReg web form of the PRP-QUANT Template V4
#' saves with "Save your current state" and reads with "Import previous state":
#' a list of `app`, `template_version`, `contributors` and `answers`. The
#' answers are the items' texts converted to plain text, with the citations
#' resolved; R1 holds the reference list. Items marked with the form's
#' not-applicable text are exported empty, with their "NA" checkbox ticked.
#' Items the web form would not show given the answers are exported empty.
#'
#' @param x A `{preregr}` (pre)registration object filled in the PRP-QUANT V4
#'   form of [form_prpquant_v4()].
#' @param file Character(1). The `.rds` file to write.
#' @param contributors A tibble of contributors, as for
#'   [write_prereg_contributors()].
#' @param bibliography Character(1). Path to the BibTeX file.
#' @param csl Character(1). Path to the citation style.
#'
#' @returns Invisibly, the state list.
prereg_to_zpid <- function(x, file, contributors, bibliography, csl) {
  items <- prereg_items(x)
  stopifnot(
    "type" %in% names(items),
    all(c("name", "affiliation", "department", "orcid", "role") %in% names(contributors))
  )
  meta <- x$form$metadata
  na_text <- meta$content[meta$field == "na_text"]
  if (length(na_text) == 0L) na_text <- "Not applicable."

  items <- items[items$id != "contributors", ]
  is_na <- !is.na(items$text) & items$text == na_text
  is_text <- items$type %in% c("text", "textarea")

  # Free text in plain form, with citations resolved; R1 gets the references
  convert <- items$shown & is_text & !is.na(items$text) & !is_na & items$id != "R1"
  converted <- prereg_convert(
    purrr::set_names(items$text[convert], items$id[convert]),
    bibliography, csl, to = "plain"
  )
  references <- prereg_convert(
    purrr::set_names(
      paste0("[@", prereg_cited_keys(x, bibliography), "]"),
      prereg_cited_keys(x, bibliography)
    ),
    bibliography, csl, to = "plain"
  )$references

  answer <- function(i) {
    id <- items$id[i]
    text <- items$text[i]
    type <- items$type[i]
    if (!items$shown[i] || is.na(text) || is_na[i]) {
      return(switch(type, radio = NULL, checkboxgroup = NULL, checkbox = FALSE, ""))
    }
    switch(
      type,
      radio = text,
      checkboxgroup = trimws(strsplit(text, ";", fixed = TRUE)[[1L]]),
      checkbox = identical(text, "Yes"),
      if (id == "R1") references else unname(converted$texts[[id]])
    )
  }

  headers <- v4_header_keys()
  answers <- list()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(items))) {
    id <- items$id[i]
    if (id %in% names(headers)) {
      answers[headers[[id]]] <- list(NULL)
    }
    answers[id] <- list(answer(i))
  }
  answers["R2"] <- list(NULL)
  answers["R3"] <- list(NULL)
  for (i in which(items$na)) {
    answers[[paste0(items$id[i], "__na")]] <- is_na[i]
  }

  state <- list(
    app = "PRP-QUANT",
    template_version = "4",
    contributors = purrr::pmap(
      contributors[c("name", "affiliation", "department", "orcid", "role")],
      \(name, affiliation, department, orcid, role) list(
        `Full name`        = name,
        Affiliation        = affiliation,
        Department         = department,
        ORCID              = orcid,
        `Contributor role` = role
      )
    ),
    answers = answers
  )

  saveRDS(state, file)
  invisible(state)
}

#' Validation expression of a PRP-QUANT V4 item
#'
#' @param type,choices See [v4_item()].
#'
#' @returns Character(1), an R expression in `VALUE`, or `NA` for free text.
v4_validation <- function(type, choices) {
  quote_vec <- function(x) paste(deparse(x), collapse = "")

  switch(
    type,
    radio = sprintf("is.na(VALUE) || (VALUE %%in%% %s)", quote_vec(choices)),
    checkboxgroup = sprintf(
      "is.na(VALUE) || all(trimws(strsplit(VALUE, ';', fixed = TRUE)[[1]]) %%in%% %s)",
      quote_vec(choices)
    ),
    checkbox = "is.na(VALUE) || (VALUE %in% c('Yes', 'No'))",
    NA_character_
  )
}


#' The PRP-QUANT Template, version 4, as a {preregr} form
#'
#' @param na_text Character(1). The text that marks an item as not applicable,
#'   which the web form records with its "NA" checkbox.
#'
#' @returns A `{preregr}` form, to pass to [preregr::prereg_initialize()]. Its
#'   items carry the extra columns `item_number`, `item_title` (the label
#'   without the star), `item_type`, `item_choices` (options separated by
#'   `" || "`), `item_required`, `item_na`, `item_shown_if_id` and
#'   `item_shown_if_value`.
form_prpquant_v4 <- function(na_text = "Not applicable.") {
  sections <- tibble::tribble(
    ~id,  ~label,
    "T",  "Title page",
    "PD", "Project documentation",
    "A",  "Abstract",
    "I",  "Introduction",
    "MD", "Method - Data collection",
    "MC", "Method - Conditions and design",
    "AP", "Analysis plan",
    "O",  "Other information",
    "R",  "References"
  )
  items <- v4_items()
  stopifnot(
    !anyDuplicated(items$id),
    all(items$section %in% sections$id),
    all(stats::na.omit(items$shown_if_id) %in% items$id),
    sum(items$required) == 24L
  )

  form <- preregr::form_create(
    title    = "Psychological Research Preregistration-Quantitative (PRP-QUANT) Template, version 4",
    version  = "4",
    author   = "Preregistration Task Force",
    date     = "2026-07-16",
    source   = "https://doi.org/10.23668/psycharchives.22316",
    comments = "Adapted for {preregr} under CC BY 4.0; see common/R/prereg-prpquant-v4.R for the changes."
  )

  form <- preregr::form_add_instruction(
    form,
    heading = "PRP-QUANT Template, version 4",
    description = paste(
      "The items follow the PreReg web form of the PRP-QUANT Template, version",
      "4 (https://doi.org/10.23668/psycharchives.22316), licensed CC BY 4.0.",
      "Required items are starred. Choice items take one of their options",
      "exactly; several options of a multiple-choice item are separated by",
      "semicolons."
    )
  )

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(sections))) {
    form <- preregr::form_add_section(
      form,
      id          = sections$id[i],
      label       = sections$label[i],
      description = NA
    )
  }

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(items))) {
    it <- items[i, ]
    choices <- it$choices[[1L]]

    description <- it$description
    if (!is.null(choices)) {
      description <- paste0(
        description, " Options: ",
        paste0("\u201c", choices, "\u201d", collapse = "; "), "."
      )
    }
    if (it$type == "checkbox") {
      description <- paste(description, "Answer \u201cYes\u201d or \u201cNo\u201d.")
    }
    if (!is.na(it$shown_if_id)) {
      description <- paste0(
        description, " Shown on the web form only if ", it$shown_if_id,
        " is \u201c", it$shown_if_value, "\u201d."
      )
    }

    form <- preregr::form_add_item(
      form,
      id          = it$id,
      label       = if (it$required) paste(it$label, "\u2605") else it$label,
      description = description,
      section_id  = it$section,
      validation  = v4_validation(it$type, choices)
    )
  }

  rows <- match(form$items$item_id, items$id)
  form$items$item_number <- items$number[rows]
  form$items$item_title <- items$label[rows]
  form$items$item_type <- items$type[rows]
  form$items$item_choices <- vapply(
    items$choices[rows],
    \(x) if (is.null(x)) NA_character_ else paste(x, collapse = " || "),
    character(1)
  )
  form$items$item_required <- items$required[rows]
  form$items$item_na <- items$na[rows]
  form$items$item_shown_if_id <- items$shown_if_id[rows]
  form$items$item_shown_if_value <- items$shown_if_value[rows]
  form$items$item_error <- ifelse(
    is.na(form$items$item_validation),
    NA_character_,
    "NAME is not one of its options."
  )
  # {preregr} names the metadata column `contents` here and copies it to
  # `content` on initialisation; appending by position works for both
  form$metadata[nrow(form$metadata) + 1L, ] <- c("na_text", na_text)

  form
}
